clue.text: Gay author in meeting with a runaway about society heiress in New York

parts.note: Willa Cather, the American novelist, is widely read as a lesbian writer
taken as written

indicators.note: the runaway goes round, or about, the letter for society

parts.note: an eloper is someone who runs away to marry

explanation.surface: A gay writer meets a runaway couple in New York society circles.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' puts S inside ELOPER, making ESLOPER. The heiress is the heroine of Henry James's Washington Square, set in New York.
explanation.definitionFit: She is the wealthy, plain daughter of Dr Sloper in Henry James's Washington Square, set in New York.

clue.text: Unsocial brute is reformed character in this 1938 historical novel

indicators.note: the three words are formed again into a new order, as a reformed character is remade

explanation.surface: An unsociable thug turns over a new leaf in a period novel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'reformed character' looks like a phrase about a changed man; 'reformed' alone signals the anagram, and the novel by Robert Graves is named after its hero, the Byzantine general.
explanation.definitionFit: Robert Graves's 1938 novel takes its title from its central figure, the Byzantine general Belisarius.

clue.text: Non-U Heep's rejected — it's not fair on him

indicators.note: rejected read as thrown back, so the shortened name is turned round
Non-U read literally: without the letter U

parts.note: Uriah is the first name of Heep, the fawning clerk in Dickens's David Copperfield

explanation.surface: An unrefined Uriah Heep is spurned because he plays unfairly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Non-U' (a British term for lower-class usage) here means drop U, leaving RIAH, which 'rejected' turns round. Uriah Heep is red-haired, so what grows on his head is not fair.
explanation.definitionFit: Heep's locks are red, so the stuff on his head is not blond: a cryptic description of what grows there.

clue.text: End up embraced by Roy? This person might

definitions.text: End up embraced by Roy? This person might

indicators.note: the turned word is held inside the name, as if hugged by it
in a down entry, up means the word is read from bottom to top, so backwards

explanation.surface: A question about a boy called Roy hugging something.
explanation.walkthrough: 'up' reverses the first word because this is a down entry, and 'embraced by' sets it inside the name. The question tail makes the whole clue describe a person so named.
explanation.definitionFit: A man's given name; the clue says the person bearing it shows the described construction in his own name.

clue.text: An author's gift for Christmas, perhaps, mistakenly "filed"

parts.note: Noel is another word for Christmas, often seen on cards
the possessive ending supplies the letter S
a treat is a gift or special present

indicators.note: the word filed is put in the wrong order, as if done in error

explanation.surface: A writer's Christmas present has been put in the wrong file.
explanation.walkthrough: 'mistakenly' rearranges FILED into FEILD, the unusual spelling of the surname. The author wrote Ballet Shoes.
explanation.definitionFit: Noel Streatfeild was an English children's writer, best known for Ballet Shoes.

clue.text: Leading characters in short story about unbelievable delays

indicators.note: the pair of first letters goes round the word for unbelievable
the leading characters of words are their first letters

parts.note: a tall story is one too far-fetched to believe

explanation.surface: The main figures in a brief tale go on about incredible holdups.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Leading characters in' takes S and S, and 'about' wraps them round TALL.
explanation.definitionFit: To stall is to hold things up, so stalls are hold-ups or postponements.

clue.text: Disabled writer's upsetting avant-garde circle

indicators.note: in a down entry, upsetting means turning the letters over, so they read backwards

parts.note: avant-garde work is new and experimental
O is the shape of a circle

explanation.surface: An injured author is troubled by an experimental literary set.
explanation.walkthrough: 'upsetting' turns NEW plus O into OWEN. Wilfred Owen, the war poet, was invalided out with shell shock; 's is a link for 'is'.
explanation.definitionFit: Wilfred Owen, the First World War poet, was sent home with shell shock and treated at Craiglockhart hospital.

clue.text: Author guesses right changes for this book of lists

indicators.note: changes signals that the letters are altered into a fresh order

explanation.surface: A writer's hunches prove correct, and he revises his reference book.
explanation.walkthrough: 'changes' rearranges AUTHOR, GUESSES and RT (right) together.
explanation.definitionFit: Peter Mark Roget's thesaurus arranges words in lists of synonyms grouped by idea.

clue.text: Perverted knight's week with Hilda in an Edwardian drama about "sin"

indicators.note: perverted means twisted out of shape, so these letters are distorted into a new order

parts.note: N is the chess abbreviation for knight, and the possessive adds S

explanation.surface: A corrupt knight spends a week with Hilda in a racy period play.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Perverted' rearranges N, S, WEEK and HILDA. Stanley Houghton's 1912 play shocked audiences because its mill girl refuses to marry the man she slept with.
explanation.definitionFit: Stanley Houghton's 1912 Lancashire play about a weekend affair caused a scandal in Edwardian theatre.

clue.text: She ran off with corny mill-owner's son

indicators.note: off read as wrong or gone bad, so the letters are scrambled

explanation.surface: A woman eloped with a man of clichéd charm, a factory heir.
explanation.walkthrough: 'off' rearranges SHE RAN and CORNY. The son is the rich young man who pursues Mary Barton in Elizabeth Gaskell's novel.
explanation.definitionFit: In Gaskell's Mary Barton he is the son of the Manchester cotton manufacturer John Carson.

clue.text: A railed pass negotiated by one noted for travelling

indicators.note: negotiated in the sense of a route worked through, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A traveller gets through a mountain pass with railings.
explanation.walkthrough: 'negotiated' rearranges A RAILED PASS. He is the narrator of Jack Kerouac's On the Road.
explanation.definitionFit: Kerouac's narrator in On the Road is famous for his journeys back and forth across America.

clue.text: Born as King? Surely not

parts.note: née marks a woman's maiden name: born as
R stands for Rex, Latin for king

explanation.surface: A doubtful query about whether someone was born royal.
explanation.definitionFit: The poetic contraction for never works as an exclamation of disbelief, much like 'never!'

clue.text: This identifies 3, 6, 9 or 12

parts.note: the numbers look like clock hours, but they point to entries in this grid, each of which is what a person is called

explanation.definitionFit: Each of those entries is what someone is called, and a label of that kind is what identifies a person.

clue.text: In Rome he brought news from me to a woman in revolution

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: in revolution means turned round, so these letters read backwards

parts.note: a lass is a young woman

explanation.surface: Someone delivers a message from the speaker to a woman during an uprising.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in revolution' turns A LASS into SSALA. In Shakespeare's Julius Caesar, this officer brings Brutus news, including Portia's death.
explanation.definitionFit: In Julius Caesar the Roman officer Messala brings Brutus reports, among them the death of Portia.

clue.text: Daniel's companion, one with a humble home, reportedly

indicators.note: reportedly means as it is spoken, so the sound of the phrase is what counts

parts.note: someone with a modest dwelling might say 'me shack', that is 'my shack'

explanation.surface: A biblical friend of Daniel lives in a modest house, so they say.
explanation.walkthrough: A poor man, in dialect, would speak of 'me shack'; said aloud that is the name. Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego were Daniel's companions in Babylon.
explanation.definitionFit: In the Book of Daniel, Meshach is one of the three companions thrown into the fiery furnace.

clue.text: Walpole and Blair (male), and more recently, Truss (female)

definitions.text: Walpole and Blair (male), and more recently, Truss (female)

parts.words: Walpole and Blair (male), and more recently, Truss (female)
parts.note: three names that suggest British prime ministers, Robert Walpole, Tony Blair and Liz Truss, but also fit Hugh Walpole, Eric Blair (George Orwell) and Lynne Truss, all writers

explanation.definitionFit: Hugh Walpole, Eric Blair and Lynne Truss all wrote books, so all are writers.

clue.text: A pub meeting with a French general and a Dickensian waiter

parts.note: a bar is a pub or a room in one
Michel Ney was one of Napoleon's marshals

explanation.surface: A tavern hosts a French general and a waiter from Dickens.
explanation.walkthrough: Barney is the waiter at the Three Cripples pub in Oliver Twist.
explanation.definitionFit: In Oliver Twist, Barney is the Jewish waiter at the Three Cripples, the thieves' public house.

clue.text: Some university students initially taking speed? Dimwitted people

indicators.note: the first letters take in, or hold, the abbreviation for speed
initially means the first letter of each of these words is taken

parts.note: mph, miles per hour, is a measure of speed

explanation.surface: Some students take drugs and seem dull-witted.
explanation.walkthrough: 'initially' takes first letters and 'taking' puts the speed unit inside them. A sumph is a Scots word for a simpleton; the surface hints at students on drugs.
explanation.definitionFit: Sumph is a Scots term for a stupid or slow person, a dolt.

clue.text: Scott's bride, sweet Charlotte the singer, who lied in part two of a novel

definitions.text: who lied in part two of a novel

parts.note: Lucy Ashton is the heroine of Walter Scott's The Bride of Lammermoor
honey is sweet, and also a term of endearment
Charlotte Church is a Welsh singer

explanation.surface: A gushing tribute links a Scott heroine and a Welsh singer to a deceitful character.
explanation.walkthrough: In part two of Forster's A Room with a View she lies to everyone, herself included, about loving George Emerson.
explanation.definitionFit: She is Forster's heroine in A Room with a View, who deceives everyone about her feelings in its second part.

clue.text: Small vehicle made an impact

parts.note: a truck is a vehicle

explanation.surface: A little lorry hit something.
explanation.definitionFit: Struck means hit, so it describes something that collided with force.

clue.text: In German cuisine, northern sweet food

parts.note: Küche is the German word for kitchen or cuisine

explanation.surface: German cooking from the north produces a dessert.
explanation.walkthrough: The umlaut of Küche is dropped in the grid.
explanation.definitionFit: Kuchen is the German word for cake, a sweet baked dish.

clue.text: Parts of masses that may be artfully scored

indicators.note: artfully suggests clever reworking, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Sections of the Mass might be cleverly set to music.
explanation.walkthrough: 'artfully' rearranges SCORED; 'scored' looks like composers' work, which helps the disguise.
explanation.definitionFit: The Credo is the statement of belief sung as one section of a sung Mass.

clue.text: "O, I could still, / Like melting snow upon some — hill, / Drop, drop, drop, drop" (Ben Jonson)

definitions.text: "O, I could still, / Like melting snow upon some — hill, / Drop, drop, drop, drop" (Ben Jonson)

parts.words: "O, I could still, / Like melting snow upon some — hill, / Drop, drop, drop, drop" (Ben Jonson)
parts.note: a quotation with a gap: the missing word is the adjective Jonson gives the hill in his song from Cynthia's Revels

explanation.definitionFit: The fill-in-the-blank quotation asks for the rugged, rocky adjective Jonson uses for the hill.

clue.text: Those exhaling excessively or inhaling dangerously

definitions.meaning: people who puff and blow out breath loudly
people who breathe in solvent or aerosol fumes to get high

explanation.definitionFit: To huff is both to blow out heavily and, in slang, to sniff fumes, so both kinds of breather fit.

clue.text: A.A. Milne's character with fine home

parts.note: Roo is Kanga's baby in Winnie-the-Pooh
F is the pencil-grade abbreviation for fine

explanation.surface: A Winnie-the-Pooh character has a nice house.
explanation.definitionFit: A roof stands for shelter or a home, as in 'a roof over your head'.

clue.text: Established company involved in crime? That's certain

definitions.meaning: settled and fixed, as in a well-established friendship
a business, and also slang for a criminal gang, as the Kray brothers' gang was known
sure and definite, as in a definite offer

explanation.definitionFit: The word means settled, a business (and slang for a criminal gang), and definite, so all three senses fit.

clue.text: A man with multiple wives and lots of 2 in 7

definitions.text: A man with multiple wives and lots of 2

indicators.note: in means the letters lie hidden inside the reference book's title

parts.note: the clue at 7 is the famous book of synonyms

explanation.surface: A polygamous man with plenty of something appears in a reference book.
explanation.walkthrough: The '2' is the answer to 2-down, what grows on the head, and '7' is the book at 7-down; the name sits inside its second word.
explanation.definitionFit: In Genesis, Jacob's brother took several wives and was born covered in red hair.

clue.text: Finally whine — scowl seems perverse otherwise

indicators.note: finally means the last letter of each of the following words is taken

explanation.surface: To end with a whinge and a frown looks contrary.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Finally' takes the last letters of WHINE, SCOWL, SEEMS and PERVERSE.
explanation.definitionFit: Else means in other circumstances, as in 'do it, or else'.

clue.text: A spell of stormy weather for Bernard in Arcadia

parts.note: a night is a spell or stretch of time
of read as in, as in a night of a storm meaning a night in it
a gale is stormy weather

explanation.surface: A stretch of storms hits a character from a Stoppard play.
explanation.walkthrough: Bernard Nightingale is the self-important academic in Tom Stoppard's play Arcadia; the songbird is a false trail.
explanation.definitionFit: In Stoppard's Arcadia, Bernard Nightingale is the don chasing a theory about Byron.

clue.text: A story of a young man aroused by the Brontë sisters?

definitions.text: A story of a young man
definitions.meaning: a verse autobiography of youth, John Betjeman's account of his early life
the sisters published as Currer, Ellis and Acton Bell, so being woken by them is being called by the Bells

explanation.definitionFit: Betjeman's 1960 verse memoir tells of his boyhood and youth, and the Brontës wrote under the surname Bell.
